opus-5.5.text:
I think that's actually one of the most interesting gaps right now. In math and code, the standards are relatively crisp. For math, you have a final answer, or a proof that can be checked. For code, you have test cases: the program either passes or it doesn't. That clarity is a big part of why reinforcement learning has worked so well in those domains. The reward signal is verifiable, so the model can explore and you can trust the feedback it gets.

Agents are much messier. When you ask what a "good agent" is, people often don't agree. Is it task completion rate? Efficiency, meaning how many steps or how much cost it takes? Robustness when the environment changes, or when a webpage looks different from what it saw in training? Whether it knows when to stop and ask the user instead of pushing ahead? All of these matter, and they often trade off against each other.

There's also the problem that many real agent tasks are open-ended. If I ask an agent to research a topic and write a report, or to plan a trip, there isn't a single correct answer. The quality depends on judgment, on what the user actually wanted, sometimes on things the user never said out loud. So evaluation drifts back toward human preference or model-as-judge setups, and those are noisier and easier to hack than a unit test.

And the environments themselves aren't standardized. In code you can spin up a sandbox and run tests reproducibly. With agents, you're dealing with browsers, APIs, operating systems, other software, and these change over time. A benchmark that made sense six months ago may already be stale, or the model may have effectively overfit to it.

So my view is that agent capability standards are still at an early, somewhat chaotic stage. That's not purely a bad thing. It means there's a lot of room for whoever can define good environments and good verifiable signals for agentic tasks. I'd even say building the evaluation and the training environments is now as important as the model itself. Whoever turns fuzzy agent goals into something closer to "checkable," the way math and code are, will probably make the next big jump in capability.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people often disagree on what makes a good agent and describes agent standards as early and chaotic, with open-ended tasks and changing environments making evaluation difficult.

r002.rationale: It contrasts math answers or proofs that can be checked and code tests that pass or fail, explaining that these verifiable signals make capability standards clearer.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that's one of the biggest differences, and I think it's underappreciated. In math and code, the standard is basically given to you. A proof is either valid or it isn't. A piece of code either passes the test cases or it doesn't. So when you do reinforcement learning in those domains, the reward signal is clean, it's cheap to verify, and you can scale it almost without limit. That's a big part of why reasoning models made such fast progress there first.

Agents are a completely different story. What does it mean for an agent to have "done well"? If I ask it to book a trip, plan a research project, or go fix something inside a large codebase, there's no single correct answer. There are many acceptable trajectories, there are tradeoffs the user cares about but never stated, and the environment itself is messy and keeps changing. So the standard isn't just unclear, it's often not fully defined until a human looks at the result and says, "yes, that's what I wanted," or "no, you missed the point."

I'd break the difficulty into a few layers. First, the outcome is multi-dimensional. Did the task get completed, but also was it efficient, was it safe, did it avoid doing anything irreversible, did it ask for help at the right moment instead of too early or too late. Second, the process matters, not just the endpoint. Two agents can reach the same final state, and one of them took a dangerous path to get there. Third, the horizon is long, so credit assignment is hard. If a task fails at step forty, which decision at step three actually caused it?

So in practice what people do right now is build environments where you can at least verify partial outcomes. Did the file end up in the right state, did the API call return the expected result, did the benchmark pass. That's borrowed from the code mindset, and it works for a subset of agent tasks. But I think the frontier is in the parts you can't verify mechanically, where you need preference data, you need model-based judges, and you need to be very careful because those judges can be gamed.

My view is that the field will converge the same way it did for math and code, just slower. Early on, nobody agreed on what a good math benchmark looked like either. The standards crystallized as the capability became real and people had to compare systems seriously. With agents we're in that earlier phase. The lack of clarity isn't a permanent property of the domain, it's a sign of how young it still is. And frankly, whoever figures out how to define and verify agent success at scale will have a huge advantage, because the training signal follows directly from that definition.

r001.rationale: The response says agent tasks have no single correct answer and that standards are often unclear until a human evaluates the result.

r002.rationale: It contrasts agents with math and code, where proofs are valid or invalid and code passes or fails test cases, presenting those checks as clear standards.

astra-6.text:
I think the standards for agent capabilities are still much less clear. In mathematics, you can usually check whether an answer is correct. In coding, you can run tests to see whether a solution meets the requirements. Those evaluations aren’t perfect, but the target is relatively explicit.

For agents, we first have to agree on what successful completion means. Are we measuring the final result, how much human intervention was needed, or whether the agent made sensible decisions along the way? An agent might reach the right result once and fail when the environment changes slightly. So success on a single task doesn’t necessarily tell us how reliable its capability is.

I think the challenge is to define tasks with clear outcomes while preserving enough of the complexity of real use. Otherwise, we risk measuring performance on a benchmark without knowing how well it translates into actually helping people.

r001.rationale: It says standards for agent capabilities are “much less clear” and explains that successful completion must first be defined.

r002.rationale: It contrasts agent evaluation with checking mathematical answers for correctness and running code tests against requirements, identifying explicit outcomes as the basis for clearer evaluation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the standards for agent capabilities are much less clear than those for mathematics and code. In mathematics, you usually have a well-defined problem and can verify whether the answer is correct. In code, you can use tests to check whether a solution meets the requirements. Those evaluations aren’t perfect, but the feedback is relatively concrete.

For an agent, even defining success can be difficult. If you ask it to conduct research or complete a complicated workflow, there may be many acceptable approaches. Do we judge the final result, the reliability of the process, the cost, or how much human intervention it needed? An agent might succeed once but fail when the environment changes slightly.

So I think we first need to make the tasks and evaluation conditions explicit: what tools the agent can use, what information it has, when it can ask for help, and what counts as completion. Otherwise, two systems can both be described as having strong agent capabilities while actually being evaluated on very different things.

r001.rationale: The response says standards for agent capabilities are much less clear and that defining success for an agent can be difficult, including in complex workflows.

r002.rationale: It explains that mathematics has well-defined problems with verifiable answers and that code can be checked with tests, making the feedback relatively concrete.
